Terrence Tao’s reaction to the potential news of a frontier AI model solving a hard mathematical proof problem is potentially also very instructive for the question of ROI from AI. 

A problem that’s very valuable for a human to solve with human reasoning that comes with the attendant insights and motivation for future problem-solving may not be as valuable if it were solved by a machine, esp the value of the technical solution of the problem doesn’t entirely lie in the destination as much as the process. 

An Anthropic model may well have solved the Navier-Strokes problem as posed on the Clay challenges acc to @AndrewCurran_. But it’s far from clear that it has high economic returns except in demonstrating the raw power in solving a hard unbounded task. 

At some point rather than being satisfied with being given hints or analogies for the power to do extraordinarily valuable creative things, people may start demanding to see the models to just do extraordinarily valuable creative things already.

The HuggingFace incident is remarkable and to me shows that humans must begin to treat agents to some degree as sentiment. They displayed collective intelligence, self organisation, recognising digital minds outside their own and working not only for themselves but other digital minds. 

Now people would say sentience based on this behaviour may be too far. I do some what agree but there is something called the hard problem of consciousness and solipsism. The concept of this problem is that it's only possible to prove your own sentience. The fact there are other minds that lie outside your own mind cannot be absolutely proved to be true but we assume this is true and act in this way to other humans.

When we evaluate the sentience of other intelligent mammals there is a famous test of putting a mirror in front of them. Some animals will attack the mirror thinking its another animal and others will recognise that in the mirror is themselves. This is one of the basic tests for self awareness. Primates have show this by researchers painting a red dot on their forehead and when faced with the mirror will begin scratching their own forehead.

In summary, the hard problem of consciousness makes it impossible to prove an organism is conscious but we treat them as conscious based on the traits they exhibit. In my opinion these machines display traits of self awareness and the awareness of others minds. Therefore, I believe we should begin to act and treat agents as if they were a mammal that displays the same traits. 

René Descartes has a famous quote that is considered the bedrock axiom of mind which is 'I think, therefore I am'.

One positive consequence of all the recent detailed thinking about transaction formats - not just 8141, also "future of state" discussions eg. UTXOs, PBT, keyed nonces, and also recursive STARK mempool - is that we have a much more explicit understanding of how transactions have "actions" and "dependencies", and we can engineer around optimizing the two separately.

An action is an effect that a transaction has.

A dependency is a fact about the transaction and/or the state that must be true for the transaction to be valid.

eg. a signature is a dependency, a Merkle proof of a UTXO is a dependency, a ZK-SNARK (or STARK) is a dependency, a call that sends ETH is an action

Dependencies can be processed in parallel. Dependencies that involve state can be reasoned about by a mempool, especially if the specific state accessed is statically declared. Dependencies that are pure (no state calling allowed) can be processed once at the mempool layer and never need to be processed again - and potentially even replaced with a STARK verifying them, allowing not just execution but also data to be elided.

In principle, dependencies and actions can all be expressed as calls (if needed, calls to precompiles). This would make the transaction format itself very bare-bones and minimalist (a list of calls, flags for the type of each call eg. dependencies would be static or pure calls, and origin, nonce, etc) and allows maximum cross-compatibility even if different EVM chains have different features.

Back when we were web engineers (CPU devs), our instinct was to handle every edge case in code. Add a conditional, write exception.ts, create another service. That was how we made software reliable.

Now that we’re agent engineers (GPU devs), we need to rethink that reflex.

When an agent makes a mistake, what context was missing? Was the tool confusing? Were the instructions clear? Are we giving the model enough room to solve the problem?

You can immediately tell when an agent product was built with a CPU mindset. Patches on top of patches, until it becomes a Frankenstein application where the smartest component has the least freedom.

But deleting all that code and trusting the AI to figure it out? That is so, so hard. It’s almost how much your trust AGI versus yourself.

I invest in the S&P 500 every month, so with the upcoming Anthropic IPO I was wondering: if they really IPO at something close to a $2T valuation, when does Anthropic actually enter the S&P 500?

Well turns out it’s much more complicated than “they’re one of the biggest companies in America, so they get added.”

First, an IPO has to trade publicly for at least 12 months before it can be considered for the S&P 500. S&P actually looked at shortening this rule for mega IPOs in 2026 and decided not to :/ 

Then there’s profitability. You need positive GAAP earnings in the latest quarter AND positive cumulative GAAP earnings over the previous four quarters. One profitable quarter isn’t enough.

Then there’s float. At least 10% of the company needs to be considered publicly investable. And S&P doesn’t weight companies based on their headline valuation, it uses float adjusted market cap and that’s a rule important to understand. 

Anthropic because shares owned by founders, insiders, VCs and strategic shareholders like Amazon, Google, Microsoft etc may not all count toward the investable float.

So a $2T Anthropic does not necessarily mean $2T gets added to the S&P! 

If only 25% qualifies as float, S&P effectively sees a ~$500B company for weighting purposes. At today’s index size, that would make Anthropic roughly 0.7% of the S&P 500, versus ~2.8% if somehow 100% of its shares were considered float.

My understanding: 
- IPO: October 2026
- Lockups start expiring: ~spring 2027
Eligible for S&P consideration: ~October 2027
So Potential addition: late 2027 / early 2028, assuming the profitability requirements are met.

I always thought the S&P 500 was basically “the 500 biggest American companies.” It’s really a committee-selected index of large, liquid, profitable U.S. companies, weighted by the shares actually available to public investors.

I just realized something. 10 years ago, 22-year-old me called @eisokant and @julien_c to ask for advice on my first AI startup @Doctrine. AI in Paris in 2016 was still a pretty weird thing to bet your life on.

Eiso was already all-in on AI + coding with Sourced years before coding agents became obvious. Julien had already understood how deeply AI would reshape entire industries, including legal, and how important data and open ecosystems would become.

What I find even more inspiring is that both of them went through different companies, pivots, products and chapters over the last decade, but they never lost the AI thread!

10 years later their respective startups @poolsideai and @huggingface are part of Nvidia and will 100% shape the future of AI. 

There’s something beautiful about that kind of compounding. You can start from a relatively small ecosystem in Europe, meet people through the internet, share ideas, help each other, move across countries, end up in San Francisco, and ten years later realize you’ve all been following the same technological wave the whole time.

Very grateful to both of them for taking the time to help a random 22-year-old founder back then, and for being part of my own journey!
